title: Killzones: when to trade
subtitle: Time of day matters as much as price

scenes.say: In forex, when you trade matters as much as where. ICT focuses on a few windows of time called killzones.

scenes.title: The trading day
scenes.say: Here's a trading day in New York time. The Asian session builds a quiet range in the evening. Then come three killzones: the London open from two to five, the New York open from seven to ten, and the London close from ten to noon.

scenes.title: The Judas swing
scenes.say: A classic pattern: shortly after midnight, price makes a false move through the Asian range, taking stops. ICT calls it the Judas swing. Then London delivers the real move the other way. On a bullish day, the London low often forms between two and five.

scenes.title: New York and the London close
scenes.say: New York then either continues London's move or reverses it, often after the eight-thirty news. Around the London close, from ten to noon, traders take profits and price can snap back. Day traders are usually done by two in the afternoon.

items.label: London open
items.sub: 2–5 am: often makes the day's high or low

items.label: New York open
items.sub: 7–10 am: continuation or reversal after 8:30 news

scenes.title: Why time matters
scenes.say: Why does it matter? Liquidity arrives at the session opens, so that's when moves are clean. A perfect level hit at the wrong hour is a lower-probability trade. Combine price with time.
points: Volume and liquidity arrive at the opens
Outside killzones, setups are lower probability
Fewer, better trades: wait for your window

els.sub: A level matters most when price reaches it at the right hour

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.say: So mark the Asian range, watch for the Judas swing, and do your trading inside the killzones. The session clock in Tools shows them live.

els.sub: London open 2–5 · New York open 7–10 · London close 10–12 (New York time)
